stories.Headline: Otter.ai raises $320 million from General Catalyst’s growth fund for its meeting tool
stories.Summary:
Otter.ai announced on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, that it raised $320 million from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund. The fund gives startups capital without diluting equity and gets returns on the results of marketing spend. Otter said it will use the money for enterprise growth, go-to-market strategy, international expansion, and product innovation. The startup has been around for nearly a decade and had raised $50 million in total funding before this, with its last round in 2021, according to PitchBook data.

Last year Otter crossed $100 million in annual recurring revenue, and the company said it is now approaching new milestones but did not provide updated figures. It said 40 million users have used its product to date, up from 25 million last year. The company did not provide numbers around monthly active users or churn. Pranav Singhvi, a partner and co-founder of the Customer Value Fund at General Catalyst, said voice is one of the biggest untapped opportunities in enterprise AI and that Otter is at the forefront of it. He said Otter helps enterprises capture critical voice data and turn it into actionable business insights, which lets teams move faster and make sharper decisions.

Otter’s newly appointed chief marketing officer, Alex Gay, who came from Superhuman, told TechCrunch at the HumanX conference last month that the company sees a big opportunity in turning transcripts into an actionable roadmap for people in back-to-back meetings. He said meetings are terribly inefficient because people spend the first twenty minutes recapping what was said before to catch everybody up. The company is now experimenting with providing insights before, after, and during meetings. It has been testing a feature to send users a pre-brief with details and background information, and it is trying out a Live Assist feature that lets users ask the AI assistant questions during a meeting.

The market is crowded with well-funded meeting notetakers like Fireflies.ai, Granola, and Read AI, along with new entrants like Calendly, Wispr, and Superhuman, which acquired Fathom. Most of these notetakers want to connect to enterprise systems and automate workflows based on data captured in meetings, and Otter is heading in that direction too. In the last few years Otter introduced a meeting assistant, a search function that works across apps, and integration with other AI tools. A challenge for Otter will be getting its customers to stick around, though the startup did not provide any numbers on that.

Articles.Title: Otter.ai raises $320 million from General Catalyst’s growth fund for its meeting tool
Otter.ai raises $320 million in non-equity financing to expand enterprise business

stories.Headline: Nvidia, Dell back $200M round for AI model developer doubleAI
stories.Summary:
DoubleAI, officially AA-I Technologies Ltd., announced on October 19, 2026 that it raised $200 million in a Series A round. Lightspeed and Bessemer co-led the round, with Nvidia Corp., Dell Technologies Inc. and several others joining. CTech reported the investment values the Tel Aviv-based company at more than $1 billion. The company has now raised $220 million in total and has about 40 employees. It was co-founded by Amnon Shashua, who is also CEO of Mobileye.

The company created an AI model called Maxwell, which it describes as its first code execution model. Maxwell applies optimizations to a program's binary rather than its source code, which removes the need for developers to manually change source code and allows applications to be modified while running in production. The model supports both graphics processing units and central processing units. It analyzes how a program interacts with its data and the underlying chips to find optimization opportunities. Maxwell is slated for broader release before the end of October.

Shashua said verifying the code was the main obstacle, and that doubleAI found a way to perform that verification formally and mathematically. He said more hardware is being built, but the need for compute is rising faster than the ability to build GPUs and CPUs, and that better hardware utilization can achieve significant savings. DoubleAI plans to bill customers according to the size of the savings it delivers. Shashua said that if the company brought a customer's compute spending down from $10 million to $6 million, it would collect a share of the $4 million saved, though he did not say what percentage. He said you cannot rely just on renting compute because prices are going up.

DoubleAI says Maxwell lowered one early customer's compute spending by 67%, according to The Wall Street Journal. The company says Maxwell sped up 55% of the algorithms in Nvidia's open-source cuGraph library by a factor of two or more, and improved pandas performance on the PDS-H benchmark by a factor of 38. It also doubled the video generation speed of a world model called LTX-2.5, and LTX CEO Zeev Farbman said Maxwell made inference for its own model twice as fast. Maxwell recently found a chess position in which 63 moves give check, beating the previous record of 60 moves, and a doubleAI agent made a new mathematical discovery about graphs. The company will use half its funding round to buy 1,000 of Nvidia's B300 Blackwell graphics cards.

Articles.Title: Nvidia, Dell back $200M round for AI model developer doubleAI
Nvidia-backed doubleAI launches AI model that cuts compute costs - Quartz

stories.Headline: Microsoft wants to limit AI agents’ permissions when they stray from the job
stories.Summary:
Microsoft announced Guardian Agents and new Playbooks on October 20, 2026, as an extension of Project Perception, its agentic security system. The company said the Guardian Agents adapt as agent activity, risk, security context and organizational policy change. They are meant to help security teams understand why risk changed, investigate evidence, recommend or apply containment measures, and strengthen policies from what they learn. People keep control over objectives and consequential decisions, according to the announcement.

The system has four ongoing responsibilities: know, contain, protect and adapt. Teams must identify agents, their owners, their purpose and their activity, contain their access and actions before they act, protect the resources they interact with, and adjust safeguards as context, behavior and risk change. Microsoft is expanding discovery to 35 additional types of local agents, bringing the total supported to 60, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and GitHub Copilot. It is also extending Microsoft Entra Agent ID with identity types for additional agent patterns, including local agents and previously unknown agents found through security sensors.

Microsoft announced Dynamic Permissions to give agents only the authority needed for an approved task, for as long as the task requires and within organization-wide policies. Those policies prevent an agent from obtaining authority its user does not have, and higher-impact actions can require verified human approval. Agents receive their own identities and task-scoped permissions, which can shrink or expire as tasks change or end, while employees retain their existing access. Microsoft also announced Dynamic Agent Risk, which combines signals from identity, data, endpoints, cloud, networks, runtime environments and the agent’s own activity, and Dynamic Conditional Access, which can preserve read access while blocking writes, narrow reachable data and resources, restrict network connections, shorten or revoke time-bound access, or require verified human approval. At the highest risk levels, it can isolate the runtime or stop execution.

Satya Nadella, CEO of Microsoft, wrote that treating frontier closed and open weight models like insider risks is a way to build such a system, not because they are necessarily malicious, but because any sufficiently capable actor with access to important systems can make mistakes or be compromised. Nadim Abdo, CVP, Identity and Network Access at Microsoft, explained that an agent can become a policy target even when it was not originally integrated with Microsoft Security. Terrell Cox, CVP and Deputy CISO, Customer Security at Microsoft, said agents will only be adopted at scale if they can be trusted at scale, and that Microsoft already operates in a world of hundreds of thousands of agents. Project Perception shares signals, context and a unified registry with Microsoft Agent 365, the company’s control plane for deploying, organizing and governing agents.

Articles.Title: Microsoft wants to limit AI agents’ permissions when they stray from the job
Microsoft Introduces New Controls to Limit AI Agent Privileges

stories.Headline: Vanina Pinto, a TAP Air Portugal Pilot: "Human Judgment Will Remain Essential in the Age of AI"
stories.Summary:
Vanina Pinto, a Senior First Officer at TAP Air Portugal, gave an interview to Dr. Adrian Leonard Mociulschi for Stiripesurse.ro, published on 19 October 2026. She said modern technology has changed pilots' work considerably, giving them more information and more accurate data for decisions. Electronic flight bags have almost completely replaced paper documentation, and modern avionics give a clearer picture of the aircraft and its surroundings. She said pilots are no longer simply flying the aircraft, since much of the job is now monitoring systems, interpreting information, managing automation and keeping situational awareness.

Pinto said judgement, decision-making, communication and adaptability are the parts of being a pilot that cannot easily be automated. Flights rarely go exactly as planned, because weather changes, technical issues occur and air traffic situations evolve, and sometimes decisions must be made with incomplete information and time pressure. She said she does not see AI replacing pilots in the foreseeable future, but rather becoming another powerful tool that can process large amounts of information, identify patterns, predict risks and help with decisions. She said the pilot will keep the final responsibility and authority for the flight, and the safest future is humans and AI working together.

A second article, in the Kyunghyang Shinmun on 19 October 2026, reported that OpenAI released as many as 722 papers claiming to have solved unsolved mathematical problems, which unsettled the global mathematics community. It said the conjecture that AI would produce new results faster than traditional peer review could vet them had become reality, and scholars now face the question of who will referee the flood of papers that will follow. It said errors pointed out in reviews by individual mathematicians led to three papers being withdrawn and 13 replaced with revised versions. It also said Professor James Maynard of the University of Oxford reviewed a claimed proof of the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, considered a Fields Medal-level problem, and reported that AI drew on research results from areas that are not entirely clear, reaffirming that AI's judgments cannot be trusted unconditionally.

Articles.Title: Vanina Pinto, a TAP Air Portugal Pilot: "Human Judgment Will Remain Essential in the Age of AI"
In the Age of AI, What Makes Humans Shine?

stories.Headline: Anthropic, Google, ByteDance & Tencent Join the Fray: Why Tech Giants Are Collectively Flocking to AI-Powered Drug Discovery
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, Google, ByteDance and Tencent have all moved into AI-powered drug discovery, according to a 36Kr report published on October 20, 2026. Anthropic has started building physical wet labs and is recruiting biochemistry talent. Google's Isomorphic Labs keeps upgrading the AlphaFold protein structure prediction model, and its latest valuation reached 40 to 50 billion US dollars. ByteDance spun off its AI pharmaceutical company Anew Labs, which raised 290 million US dollars in a first round at a post-investment valuation of about 1.5 billion US dollars.

The article says AI compresses drug discovery time by 30 to 50 percent, and that AI-discovered molecules reach 80 to 90 percent success in Phase I trials against a historical average of 52 percent. More than 170 AI drug projects worldwide have entered clinical stages, and 7 AI drugs have entered or completed Phase III trials. Isomorphic Labs' IsoDDE engine is said to cut a search of 10^60 chemical spaces from several years to several days. Insilico Medicine's Rentosertib, found with AI help, has entered Phase III trials for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, predicted that AI could overcome most serious diseases in the next 5 to 10 years. Demis Hassabis of Google DeepMind has said the best use of AI is to improve human health, and he shared half of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for AlphaFold. The US FDA said digital transformation will not change existing CGMP requirements and that quality oversight cannot be transferred because of AI. No AI drug has yet passed regulatory approval and reached the market.

The 36Kr article notes that AI mainly changes the upstream discovery stage, which accounts for only 38 percent of costs, while 62 percent goes to clinical trials and approval. It names high-quality data as the biggest bottleneck, since failed molecule data held by drug companies and CROs is rarely made public. Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs and Meta plan to invest 1.8 billion US dollars in a next-generation biological AI model and open data infrastructure. A separate Yahoo Finance article says Tencent joined ByteDance and Alibaba in placing large 2026 orders for Nvidia high-end AI chips, with combined orders exceeding Nvidia's planned output.

Articles.Title: Anthropic, Google, ByteDance & Tencent Join the Fray: Why Tech Giants Are Collectively Flocking to AI-Powered Drug Discovery - 36Kr
What Do Tencent Holdings (SEHK:700) Chip Orders Mean For Its AI Push?

stories.Headline: New AICPA Joint Offering Provides Full Review of Business Risk Related to AI Systems and Agents
stories.Summary:
The American Institute of CPAs teamed with the Artificial Intelligence Underwriting Company on a new assurance certification, announced in a media release on Oct. 19. The offering is called SOC 2 plus AIUC-1, and the two partners say it provides the first comprehensive, independent review of business risk related to AI systems and agents. It pairs CPA assurance rigor with the AIUC's frontier AI technical testing. Last year, more than 40,000 organizations obtained a SOC 2 attestation or an AIUC-1 certification.

The offering combines a SOC 2 report with an AIUC-1 certification in one CPA-led engagement. SOC 2 is an independent examination performed by a licensed CPA under AICPA attestation standards, and it evaluates controls for security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, or privacy. AIUC-1 was developed by a consortium of more than 250 chief information security officers and security leaders from Fortune 1000 companies, and it is updated quarterly. Its controls span six principles, which are data and privacy, security, safety, reliability, accountability, and society, and they map to frameworks such as MITRE ATLAS, ISO 42001, and the EU AI Act. Both SOC 2 reports and AIUC-1 certifications require annual renewal, and AIUC-1 also requires quarterly technical retesting.

AICPA President and CEO Mark Koziel said companies have made substantial investments in AI, and investors, clients, and other stakeholders deserve a fuller, objective picture of whether the technology is safe, reliable, and properly governed. He said the joint offering delivers that, and with CPAs leading the engagement, organizations can use the expertise, integrity, and professional judgment that builds trust across capital markets. AIUC co-founder Rajiv Dattani said AI agents do real work faster than anyone can check it, and the certification answers two questions every organization now asks, which are what its security posture is and whether its agents behave as intended. He said AIUC-1 stands apart through live testing of agent behavior rather than just a review of policies and guardrails, with agents tested across hundreds of risk and attack combinations, from hallucinations and data leakage to manipulative requests and adversarial prompt injection.

The AICPA said AI misfires have raised serious concerns about safety and security in critical business operations, and AI agents now hold credentials, call APIs, and act inside core systems, so an AI failure is increasingly a security breach. It also said trust is negotiated one security questionnaire at a time, a slow and costly exchange that rarely settles the question and hinders AI adoption. Several CPA firms are now delivering the joint SOC 2 plus AIUC-1 offering to clients. Once initial engagements have concluded, a full launch of the joint certification is expected in early 2027.

Articles.Title: New AICPA Joint Offering Provides Full Review of Business Risk Related to AI Systems and Agents
AICPA partners on new offering that assures AI systems and agents

stories.Headline: Azerbaijan warns of AI-driven information security risks
stories.Summary:
Azerbaijan warned about new information security risks from artificial intelligence at a summit in Baku on Tuesday, October 20, 2026. Lieutenant General Allahveran Ismayilov, Deputy Chief of the State Service for Special Communication and Information Security, spoke at the 8th Summit of Heads of Information Security for State Institutions. He said AI is used to craft more convincing phishing attacks, refine social engineering, forge audio and visual content, spread disinformation, and carry out existing cyber threats on a larger scale. The event was reported by Trend News Agency.

Ismayilov said uncontrolled use of public AI tools, transfers of sensitive data to external platforms, reliance on cloud services and third-party providers, and uncertainty about how AI systems collect, process, and store data all create additional risks. He said implementing AI is not a standalone technology decision but a strategic issue affecting governance, risk assessment, and data protection. He said the role of information security leaders is growing because they must anticipate risks from new technologies and help enable secure innovation. He noted that the Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Azerbaijan for 2025, 2028 provides a framework, and that identifying and assessing AI risks in government institutions is particularly important.

Ismayilov said the application of AI in public administration, the expansion of digital capabilities, and governance mechanisms in this field are key priorities for Azerbaijan. He said the task is to use AI's potential while ensuring its reliability, security, and responsible management. The summit aims to share experience among information security heads of state institutions, strengthen cooperation on information security and cybersecurity, and discuss modern technological challenges and AI use. Topics include integrating AI into public administration and digital infrastructure, emerging cyber threats, principles for a reliable and secure digital state, data management, and managing information security and cybersecurity risks.

A separate Dark Reading article described related risks in enterprises that use a mix of generative AI models, agents, and AI-connected tools. It said seven in 10 surveyed security leaders say AI tools have access to core business systems, yet few say they govern that access effectively. Mounir Hahad, Head of HPE Threat Labs, said enterprise AI is becoming a system rather than a single model, with routers choosing among models, workflows launching agents, and models running from laptops to vendor clouds. The article said individual actions by approved models may look benign while combined actions across systems could be malicious, and that attackers use AI for reconnaissance, phishing, vulnerability research, code development, and command generation, including synthetic voices and deepfake videos for executive impersonation fraud.

Articles.Title: Azerbaijan warns of AI-driven information security risks
The hidden risks of fragmented AI security - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: Nvidia, German government team to advance industrial AI
stories.Summary:
At the Invest in Germany summit in Berlin on 20 October 2026, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang revealed a joint initiative to advance edge AI models for physical AI. The declaration sets out an agreement for the German federal government to work with Nvidia to formalise and expand Nvidia's collaboration with Germany and its Industry 4.0 platform. Merz said his government aims to make Germany one of the most advanced places in the world, not just in the European Union, to work with AI and integrate it into industry. Huang said Nvidia's relationship with German industry began in the early 2000s by supplying technology for gaming systems, workstations and automotive design, and has evolved to partnerships in autonomous vehicle development and digital twins for manufacturing.

According to media reports first cited by Handelsblatt, the federal government plans to contribute a nine-figure sum to the partnership. Around a dozen German companies are expected to join the government-backed project, including Siemens, Audi and AI start-up Black Forest Labs from Freiburg im Breisgau. Nvidia said it invested almost one billion dollars in Germany in 2025 and holds stakes in numerous German start-ups and established firms. At the summit, Amazon also announced plans to invest around 16 billion euros in Germany in 2027, with one third, or 4.8 billion euros, going mainly to the Frankfurt am Main region to expand data centres for its cloud provider AWS. Amazon said around 3,000 employees already work for AWS in Germany.

Merz called on companies in Germany to open their industrial data for artificial intelligence to safeguard the competitiveness of sectors such as the car industry, arguing that preserving Germany's industrial base is a crucial advantage over other economies. He said Germany's biggest advantage is its Mittelstand, small and medium businesses, and urged them to open their doors for AI to make use of their data. Huang said national expertise and knowledge set the German economy apart and that AI will only amplify it, adding that AI can augment capability but will not replace it. Huang also said it pained him to see how far Germany had fallen behind, and advised the country to simply get to work.

Nvidia announced AI solutions at Siemens' Erlangen factory that cut production engineering effort by up to 85% and manufacturing costs by up to 20%, and an expanded partnership with Mercedes-Benz to co-develop next-generation automated driving systems using Nvidia's Hyperion, Alpamayo and Halos technologies alongside Mercedes-Benz's MB.OS platform. Nvidia is also using Jupiter, Europe's first exascale supercomputer at the Jülich Supercomputing Centre, to run a 104-qubit fault-tolerant quantum computing simulation that validates a magic state cultivation approach, claimed to require 90% fewer qubits than previous methods. Nvidia announced planned investments in four German startups in physical AI: Agile Robots, Avelios Medical, Mirelo and Reflex Aerospace. The International Monetary Fund now expects growth of 1.3 percent in Germany in 2026, after previously forecasting only 0.7 percent, and whether further upswing materialises thanks to investment by US tech giants remains to be seen.

Articles.Title: Nvidia, German government team to advance industrial AI
Investment summit: German government strikes AI deal with Nvidia

stories.Headline: Abiologics Appoints Per Jr. Greisen as Chief Artificial Intelligence Officer - Carroll County Mirror-Democrat
stories.Summary:
Abiologics announced on Oct. 20, 2026, that it had appointed Per Jr. Greisen, Ph.D., as its Chief Artificial Intelligence Officer. The company is based in Watertown, Massachusetts, and is a Flagship Pioneering company that uses generative AI and chemical synthesis to develop therapeutics beyond the limits of biology. Greisen is described as an AI protein design pioneer. He joins to advance the company's platform for de novo generation of synthetic D-protein therapeutics.

In the role, Greisen will lead Abiologics' AI and machine learning strategy. He will work to advance the platform for de novo generation of Synteins, which are programmable D-protein therapeutics with advantaged pharmacological properties. He will also drive the industrialization, design and development of this new generation of biologics. The company says its platform combines the first generative AI model capable of designing synthetic D-protein therapeutics de novo with the only automated chemical synthesis and wet lab screening process able to test hundreds of candidate Synteins every week. Its foundation is the only scaled, AI-driven, closed-loop experimental dataset for D-proteins, built exclusively from proprietary binding and developability data that cannot be found publicly.

Avak Kahvejian, Ph.D., Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Abiologics, President of Flagship Labs and General Partner at Flagship Pioneering, said the company was thrilled to welcome Greisen. He said designing proteins beyond nature's conventional building blocks gives therapeutics supranatural pharmacological properties but requires fundamentally new approaches to generative AI, computational design and lab automation. He said Greisen's experience at the intersection of artificial intelligence, physics-informed modeling and protein engineering uniquely positions him to lead the platform into its next chapter. Greisen said Abiologics is tackling one of the most compelling challenges in AI-driven drug discovery by building its protein design platform from first principles. He said the chance to help define a field and create a new therapeutic modality drew him to the company, and he is thrilled to join the team to expand what protein medicines can achieve for patients.

Greisen was a postdoctoral fellow in the laboratory of David Baker and has held multiple senior industry roles since. He most recently served as Chief Scientist of AI Biology at BioMap, where he led a team integrating data-driven AI with computational protein design. Before that, he was VP of Computational Drug Design at Novo Nordisk, where he built and scaled the company's digital science and innovation divisions and led teams using AI and machine learning algorithms to discover therapeutic candidates for metabolic diseases and rare bleeding disorders. His work spans generative modeling, de novo protein design and translational AI platforms, contributing to clinical- and commercial-stage protein therapeutics including antibodies, bispecifics and peptides. Abiologics was founded by Flagship Labs, the innovation foundry of Flagship Pioneering, in 2021.

Articles.Title: Abiologics Appoints Per Jr. Greisen as Chief Artificial Intelligence Officer - Carroll County Mirror-Democrat
Abiologics Appoints Per Jr. Greisen as Chief Artificial Intelligence Officer

stories.Headline: Seoul stocks extend losses late Tues. morning amid AI concerns - Yonhap News Agency
stories.Summary:
Seoul stocks fell sharply on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, as concerns about investments in the artificial intelligence value chain led to a sell-off in major chip shares. The benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index, or KOSPI, dropped 215.27 points, or 3.73 percent, to close at 5,552.74 after falling as low as 5,493.24. The index had opened 0.6 percent lower and extended its losses during the session. The KOSPI had risen for two straight sessions before Tuesday, following a steep sell-off driven by worries about AI-related investments. It had plunged about 21 percent over seven trading sessions from October 6 through Thursday.

Trade volume was light at 259.75 million shares worth 16 trillion won, or about 12.97 billion dollars, with 771 declining stocks against 117 advancing ones. Foreigners sold a net 535.4 billion won and institutions sold 1 trillion won, while individual investors bought a net 900 billion won. Samsung Electronics fell 2.98 percent to 211,500 won, and SK hynix declined 4.23 percent to 1.22 million won, heading for its lowest close since April. SK Square, the parent firm of SK hynix, dipped 5 percent to 741,000 won, and Samsung Electro-Mechanics went down 1.28 percent to 1.16 million won. The Korean won was quoted at 1,328.1 won against the U.S. dollar, up 2.2 won from the previous session, while the three-year Treasury yield fell 3.7 basis points to 3.840 percent and the five-year yield declined 2.4 basis points to 3.990 percent.

Lee Kyoung-min, an analyst at Daishin Securities, said concerns over credit risks and profitability surrounding AI investment had not been fully resolved, which limited the sustainability of the rebound. He said profit-taking emerged following the previous session's gains, sending the market back into negative territory. The article also linked the reduced appetite for risky assets to escalating protests in France. Overnight in the U.S., stocks ended mixed as technology shares rebounded from their steepest weekly drop since June. The Dow Jones Industrial Average edged down 0.07 percent, while the S&P 500 rose 0.41 percent and the Nasdaq Composite gained 1.11 percent to finish at 26,430.89.

Articles.Title: Seoul stocks extend losses late Tues. morning amid AI concerns - Yonhap News Agency

stories.Headline: Inception Releases Mercury 3 Diffusion LLM at 1,068 Tokens per Second
stories.Summary:
Inception released Mercury 3 on Monday, October 20, 2026, according to the articles. It is the company's fourth Mercury model, following Mercury 1, Mercury 2 and Mercury 2.5. Mercury 1 launched in 2025, and Mercury 2.5 added tunable reasoning and a 260K context window. Mercury 3 is a diffusion LLM that writes answers in parallel rather than token by token. Inception reports 1,068 tokens per second on NVIDIA GPUs and a 1M-token context window.

The model is API only, with no open weights or quantized builds, and Inception did not disclose its parameter count. Inception says it is more than 40x larger than Mercury 1, and average quality rose about 3x between the two models. On Inception's own benchmark table, Mercury 3 leads GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 on 8 of 12 tests, including SWE-Bench Atlas at 51.08 and IFBench at 76.84. It trails on DeepSWE v1 at 46.31 and MRCR v2 at 75.50. Launch pricing is $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.35 per million output tokens, which is 50% off the eventual standard price of $0.20 and $0.70.

CEO Stefano Ermon told The Deep View that Mercury 3 is the most capable diffusion-based language model on the market. He said it is comparable to the Luna and Haiku models but way faster, at 1,000 tokens per second, and almost instant. Ermon also said the company is working on developments that could make the launch price permanent in the weeks ahead. Inception reported that swarms of Mercury 3 agents used for recursive self improvement raised overall speed by 16% on top of its own upgrades.

The articles say diffusion models start from a rough draft of the full answer and refine every position over a few passes in parallel, which means fewer sequential steps and faster output on the same GPUs. Inception's early-access partners include TinyFish, which ran 50 live Mind2Web web-navigation tasks, and Octen AI, which reported 0.9 seconds median generation. The Deep View notes that Google DeepMind released DiffusionGemma in June with 26 billion parameters. It says the open question is whether diffusion LLMs remain a niche for real-time applications or become a long-term challenger to frontier models.

stories.Headline: ASHG: Long-Read Genomics Meets Clinical Data in PacBio, Verily Health AI Deal - Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology News
stories.Summary:
PacBio and Verily Health announced a multi-year strategic collaboration on October 19, 2026, to combine PacBio's HiFi long-read sequencing with Verily's clinical data and cloud-based analysis. The companies said the arrangement is meant to produce clinico-genomic datasets for biomedical research and for training and deploying artificial intelligence models. Under the agreement, PacBio sequencing workflows will be connected with Verily Pre, a platform for governing, analyzing, and using health data. Verily will configure the platform's Workbench research environment to aggregate, analyze, and curate HiFi genomic datasets alongside real-world clinical information.

The collaboration will focus on connecting long-read data with clinical records, which can otherwise require separate tools and customized workflows. Verily Pre already supports population-scale biomedical research, and its Workbench serves more than 20,000 researchers and has supported more than 700 publications. PacBio HiFi whole-genome sequencing workflows already run end-to-end within the Verily Pre environment, giving the expanded work a technical starting point. The companies also plan to use Verily Pre's trusted agentic environment for AI model training and inference. The announcement did not disclose financial terms, specific customers, or a timetable for broader deployment.

Stephen Gillett, chairman and CEO of Verily Health, said the collaboration reflects a shared focus on making high-quality genomic data more accessible and useful across research and development. He said the companies hope to deliver a meaningful impact to researchers and innovators working to find new answers for neurology, oncology, rare disease, and other areas of critical unmet need. Mark Van Oene, president and CEO of PacBio, said HiFi sequencing offers customers complete and high-quality data, which he said is ideal for training AI models where the input determines the success of the output. He said the collaboration is building a path to turn richer biological data into AI-ready data at scale.

Long-read sequencing can capture structural variants, methylation patterns, and full-length RNA transcripts that may be difficult to resolve with short-read methods. The companies said biomedical AI models increasingly require biological data with greater depth, context, and scale, while processing large, complex datasets and integrating them with clinical data remains fragmented and largely bespoke. Over the course of the collaboration, the companies plan to extend the integration to support increasingly large and complex long-read programs across research organizations, biopharma companies, clinical institutions, and population genomics programs. They envision a common infrastructure that can scale with those programs and support multimodal research and AI development.

Dave McKay, the president and chief executive of Royal Bank of Canada, said he is considering blocking Meta Platforms Inc.'s artificial intelligence agent Muse from the bank's customer information. He made the comment on Bloomberg Surveillance in an interview reported on 20 October 2026. McKay said the bank has to protect the consumer and that the organization is liable. The agent is described in the report as popular.

The step under consideration would stop Muse from reaching RBC customer data. McKay framed the issue as a matter of consumer protection and of the bank's own liability as an organization. The report gives no date for a decision and no details of how a block would work. It also gives no figures on how many customers or accounts could be affected.

McKay is the person responsible for the bank's position, as president and chief executive, and he set out his reasoning in the interview. He said, in paraphrase, that protecting the consumer comes first and that the bank carries liability for that protection. The articles do not say whether Meta has responded or been asked about the plan. They also do not say whether other banks are weighing similar moves.

The articles give little beyond McKay's comment, so what happens next is not yet known. It is not clear when RBC might decide or what a block would mean for customers who use Muse. Meta has not commented in the reports, and no regulator is named. More to follow.

stories.Headline: MiniMax launches M3.1 Flash model, says it cuts AI agent costs by 70%
stories.Summary:
MiniMax, a Hong Kong-listed artificial intelligence developer, launched its new M3.1 Flash text model on October 19, 2026. The company says the model reduces overall usage costs by 70 percent and marks its first text-model release in four months. MiniMax also revealed that an anonymous model called Space Bunny, which processed more than 200 trillion tokens, was an early version of M3.1 Flash. The model is described as delivering what the company calls a generational leap in agentic tasks, coding, computer use, and cybersecurity.

The M3.1 Flash is a 428 billion parameter mixture-of-experts model with API pricing set at $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output tokens. Its open weights are due on October 23, 2026, and the model was free on OpenRouter for the first 72 hours after launch. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, it scores 42, which is 13 points higher than the previous MiniMax M3 and less than half the cost per task. It scores level with GLM-5.3 Flash but behind DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, and on one business benchmark it scored 62.2 percent compared with 50.3 percent for Opus 5 and 45.8 percent for GPT-5.6 Sol.

MiniMax said the model achieves frontier-level intelligence across key tasks while redefining the performance economics of agentic AI. The company also confirmed that Space Bunny was an early version of M3.1 Flash and that it has continued improving the model since then. A MiniMax representative said the team is excited about finding a balance between intelligence, speed, and cost. The company is preparing to release a Pro model soon, which Reuters and The Information report is expected to have a total of 2.7 trillion parameters.

The launch adds to intensifying price competition among Chinese AI startups and technology giants, which are rolling out cheaper Flash models as computing costs rise and share prices weaken. Space Bunny had been OpenRouter's top model for 10 straight days and processed 56.7 trillion tokens before leaving the platform on October 5. MiniMax M3.1 Flash is now live in the Code Arena WebDev benchmark, where it debuted at number 12 among open models with 1,588 points, a 106 point increase from the previous MiniMax M3. The company has not yet announced a specific release date for the upcoming Pro model.

stories.Headline: TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever
stories.Summary:
On October 19, 2026, Hugging Face announced TorchNeuron, a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. The work came from Régis Pierrard, Simon Pagezy, Michael Benayoun, Jingya Huang, Alvaro Moran, David Corvoysier and Jeff Boudier. TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that supports eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Starting October 20, 2026, it will be available as a public beta, installable with pip install torch-neuronx.

The change makes Trainium a device like any other for Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL, so the same classes and scripts work as on other accelerators. Hugging Face now recommends Neuron users go through these libraries directly instead of Optimum Neuron. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. Users pass device_map=neuron to move a model to Neuron devices, and a static cache is strongly recommended to prevent frequent recompilations.

Training uses the same libraries as any other accelerator, with no dedicated trainer or Neuron-specific fork of model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on Trainium with a few Neuron-specific settings, including static shapes, torch.compile on, and async weight loading off via HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1. Hugging Face ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips, which is 32 NeuronCores or half a trn2.48xlarge instance, using TP_SIZE=4 and FSDP_SIZE=8 for 32 processes. The saved checkpoint is a standard Transformers checkpoint that can be pushed to the Hub and loaded on other hardware.

Separately, Deepgram worked with the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering team over several months to port its Nova-3 speech-to-text model to Trainium2 for offline batch workloads such as contact-center analytics and medical transcription. The final setup runs eight model replicas on a single trn2.3xlarge instance and processed 11, 70 percent more audio per dollar than the compute options Deepgram had been running. Deepgram built a data-parallel Rust runtime that calls Trainium without Python or PyTorch in the serving path, delivering a 7.5% throughput gain over the multiprocessing Python baseline. The articles say more Diffusers pipelines will become compatible with tensor parallelism, and more Neuron kernels will appear on the Hub.

stories.Headline: The hidden risks of fragmented AI security
stories.Summary:
Enterprises are adopting a growing mix of generative AI models, agents, and AI-connected tools, often within the same environment, and this is increasing the cyber-attack surface. Seven in 10 surveyed security leaders say AI tools have access to their organization’s core business systems, yet few say they govern that access effectively. Security efforts often focus on individual models and applications, but Mounir Hahad, Head of HPE Threat Labs, says enterprise AI is becoming a system, not a single model. In this AI stack, routers choose among models, workflows launch agents, and models run anywhere from laptops to vendor clouds. The challenge is to understand how the different AI systems work together, and how their combination creates risk exposure that no single control can identify.

Governance typically defines policies for AI use, such as which agents can run in the environment and what Model Context Protocol servers they can connect to, but these policies enforce behavior component by component. They miss what happens when several approved components act together, and an approved task by a sanctioned model may look benign on its own while combined actions by multiple agents could lead to something malicious. Research has shown that a model’s refusal behavior can weaken substantially without retraining, and safety-stripped versions of well-known open models are already circulating publicly. Organizations also approve a model once and rarely revisit that decision, yet models can evolve after updates, new integrations, or shifts in use. Hahad says there are easy ways to circumvent guardrails, so the final check has to be outside the model, not within it.

Hahad says many organizations are scared of deploying AI agents within their networks but have no choice, at the risk of being left behind by their competitors. He says the cybersecurity vendor industry needs time to absorb the changes coming at breakneck speed and provide solutions that truly defend against this new attack surface. He calls this a pivotal moment when collaboration between security vendors through industry groups like the Cyber Threat Alliance will accelerate the global response time. The likely model in the short term is shared responsibility, similar to cloud adoption, with security vendors building stronger visibility, enforcement, and threat intelligence into their platforms while enterprises remain responsible for how they use AI.

Threat actors are already taking advantage of AI for reconnaissance, phishing, vulnerability research, code development, and command generation. Adversaries have been observed using generative AI to produce synthetic voices and deepfake videos for targeted executive impersonation fraud. Malware such as LAMEHUG queries hosted large language models to generate real-time commands for reconnaissance, data theft, and system manipulation rather than relying on hardcoded logic. Anthropic reported disrupting an espionage campaign where AI reportedly carried out 80 to 90 percent of the tactical operations, with human operators setting strategy and approving key decisions. Based on nearly 1,200 active threat campaigns tracked globally in 2025, the HPE Threat Labs 2026 Report found that attackers are still exploiting vulnerabilities that are years old, with AI sharpening tradecraft that already works.

stories.Headline: How smart will Hong Kong’s ‘AI city brain’ be?
stories.Summary:
Hong Kong authorities plan to build an AI-powered urban management system, and officials told a Legislative Council meeting on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, that the first phase will focus on infrastructure monitoring. The project is expected to cost HK$200 million and will integrate infrastructure databases before exploring expansion into public services. Undersecretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry Lillian Cheong Man-lei said authorities would prioritise several databases monitoring city infrastructure conditions. These include the Lands Department's geospatial database and its underground utilities system, which maps water, natural gas pipes and electricity grid conditions.

The first phase requires government arms to develop their own databases before connecting them to the "AI city brain." The system aims to link databases on landslide monitoring, fallen trees, water pipes, weather and public complaints, among others. Handling extreme weather will be the first scenario to test the initiative. The government says it is drawing lessons from mainland cities as it builds the system.

Cheong is the official named as leading the priority work on infrastructure databases. Officials said government arms are encouraged to develop their own databases before connecting them to the system. The government says it is drawing lessons from mainland cities, while scholars caution that Hong Kong must not simply copy their formulas. The articles do not say who else is responsible for the project.

The context is Hangzhou's AI urban management system, which has been in place and evolving for more than a decade. When Severe Typhoon Dolphin approached eastern China in August, more than 110,000 delivery riders across Hangzhou received automatic alerts and personalised safety guidance on their mobile phones every minute. Hangzhou's "riders' code" system navigated them to the nearest shelters, which authorities said had reduced their occupational risks under extreme weather. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the first phase and later exploration of public services.

stories.Headline: 3D TSV and 2.5D Market to Reach USD 21.50 Billion by 2035 as High-Bandwidth Memory Stacks Advance
stories.Summary:
Credence Research published a report on October 19, 2026, estimating that the global 3D TSV and 2.5D market was worth USD 9.46 billion in 2025 and will reach USD 21.50 billion by 2035. The report states a compound annual growth rate of 8.50% for 2026 to 2035. North America held the largest regional share at 35.0% in 2025, while the Middle East and Africa is the fastest-growing region at a modeled 9.96% annual rate. All market sizes, segment shares and regional allocations are Credence Research estimates.

The market covers through-silicon-via stacking and silicon-interposer packaging work used in HBM, logic, image sensors, MEMS and RF devices. It excludes the value of semiconductor dies, fabrication equipment, bridge-only packages without TSVs and fan-out packages without vias. HBM and other memory accounted for 46.0% of 2025 application revenue, and 2.5D integration led technology categories with 38.0% of 2025 value. Data centers and high-performance computing held 55.0% of end-use spending, die-to-wafer integration accounted for 48.0% of value, and Asia Pacific held 33.0% of demand while hosting much of the production capacity.

SK hynix, Samsung Electronics and Micron are named as leading HBM stacking manufacturers, TSMC provides silicon-interposer integration, and ASE Technology Holding and Amkor Technology perform advanced assembly and test. The report says Intel and JCET participate in adjacent packaging approaches but does not establish their specific TSV revenue. On June 16, 2026, TSMC and Amkor announced a 10-year agreement for advanced packaging and testing services in Arizona, with no financial terms disclosed. On February 12, 2026, Samsung Electronics announced it had begun mass production and commercial shipments of HBM4.

The report says AI accelerators use multiple HBM stacks beside processor dies, raising demand for more vias and larger interposers per package, and that memory bandwidth has become a central constraint in AI system design. It notes that packaging investment in the United States and Asia is expanding capacity, though new plants require long qualification periods and can face construction delays. The principal risks listed are concentration among a small group of AI buyers, plant timing and the cost of new bonding and thermal processes. Mature image-sensor and MEMS applications are described as a more stable but slower-growing base.

stories.Headline: US Navy, Gecko Robotics surge AI maintenance contract to $300M
stories.Summary:
Gecko Robotics announced on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, that the U.S. Navy is increasing the value of its initial contract to up to $300 million. The deal comes just six months after the company reached its first agreement with the sea service. The initial contract began as a 5-year, $54 million indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity deal. Under that deal, Gecko works on 18 ships assigned to the Navy's U.S. Pacific Fleet.

The company uses drones, wall-climbing robots and fixed sensors to gather data on components, decks, welds and hulls. That information, paired with AI tools, is used to identify current and potential structural issues that may remain hidden to the naked eye. A key part of the new investment is Gecko's Komodo machine system, which analyzes the health of deck coatings by scanning and eliminates the need to physically dig into them. This lets the Navy plan repairs and map out damaged areas before a ship enters dry dock, something that previously only happened after the maintenance cycle began. Gecko said in a release that its technology can save the Navy up to $8 million in repair costs per ship and identify structural issues up to 50 times faster than traditional methods, reducing inspections from months to days.

Gecko Robotics is the company behind the technology and announced the increased contract value. Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle, who adopted the 80% readiness goal from his predecessor Adm. Lisa Franchetti, wrote for Military Times in December that reaching it requires shorter maintenance cycles, increased spare-parts availability, improved training pipelines and targeted upgrades across the fleet.

The Navy has consistently stated its goal of reaching 80% fleet readiness by 2027, despite criticisms of its deployment capabilities. The Government Accountability Office reported in December 2024 that readiness rates among the Navy's amphibious warfare ships fell to 46% between 2011 and 2020, hindering Marine Corps deployment and training plans. In August 2025, that rate reportedly dipped to just 41%, resulting in a more than five-month gap in Marine Expeditionary Unit deployments that year. That gap further strained resources amid the Trump administration's push to counter the illicit drug trade in Latin America and the Caribbean.

stories.Headline: A profile of Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national who the FBI arrested after OpenAI discovered a recording device and who has deep connections in Saudi Arabia (Financial Times)
stories.Summary:
Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35 year old Saudi national and engineer at OpenAI, was arrested by the FBI on 9 October after a hidden recording device was found in an executive conference room at the company’s San Francisco office. An OpenAI employee discovered the device around 30 September, plugged into a USB port behind a television and wrapped in toilet paper. The device was believed to have been placed there around 28 September, and its stored data was encrypted. Alfozan was not authorised to access the conference room where the device was found. Surveillance footage showed Alfozan near the room several times before the device was discovered, and on 5 October he allegedly entered the room to retrieve it.

An unattended bag belonging to Alfozan was also found on 5 October, containing his wallet, identification, and another recording device similar to the one discovered in the conference room. He was charged with using, or attempting to use, an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. According to his LinkedIn profile, Alfozan worked as an engineering leader at OpenAI and holds a degree in computer science and engineering from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. FBI Director Kash Patel said that, according to the complaint, Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer’s executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s superintelligence technology. OpenAI said Alfozan had planted the device a few days before it was discovered and that the FBI moved quickly to make an arrest.

The company said it had terminated his employment. OpenAI also said it had no indications that he inappropriately accessed or exfiltrated model weights, source code, or customer data. OpenAI said it takes protecting its technology, data, and people seriously and treats the matter as one of national importance. The company said it used its models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it. The articles do not say what will happen next in the legal case beyond the arrest and charge.

stories.Headline: AI Companies Have Piled On $88 Billion in Junk Debt This Year. Are Lenders Now Getting Nervous?
stories.Summary:
Low-rated companies have issued $88 billion of AI-related debt this year, according to Goldman Sachs. In the first 11 months of 2025, the number was about $20 billion, per Neuberger Berman. Now lenders are getting picky, and unproven AI borrowers face higher rates and tougher terms. Investors want companies with real assets and steady contracts, and that shift says something about where AI is heading. It is not just a software story anymore, but an expensive physical buildout.

Not every AI borrower is getting the same deal, and lenders are demanding more from companies that have not proven they can pay. Even big names are paying up, and SoftBank Group, which is rated just below investment grade, recently paid as much as 9.75% to borrow. Meanwhile, the money is flowing to the hard stuff, and AI infrastructure debt from lower-rated borrowers has hit $40 billion this year, according to BNP Paribas, up from $12 billion in all of 2025. Data centers are doing much of that borrowing, and lenders do not want to bet on promises but on things they can touch.

Tech expert James Altucher points to one small company he says already owns a piece of that buildout Elon Musk cannot skip. He says Musk is not renting the pieces he needs from someone else but building them himself, including rockets, launch sites, satellites, the AI itself and a planned chip factory. Altucher points to a SpaceX filing with the FCC that he says shows how far Musk plans to take it, with a million AI data center satellites running in orbit. By Altucher's count, Musk is just getting started, and they have only accomplished 1% of what Elon has set out to do, he says.

Altucher believes he has found one answer in a small supplier that he says helped create the nervous system for Musk's satellites. He says the two have a jointly created, patent protected system that is being used in Elon's satellites, and it is not a new relationship. This is not some company hoping Elon calls one day, Altucher says, because they already have him and have for over a decade. AI takes a massive physical machine to build, and the best opportunities may be far from the famous names.

stories.Headline: Everlaw Survey: In-House Legal Teams Are Using AI to Cut Law Firm Spend and 81% Expect Outcome-Based Pricing to Eclipse the Billable Hour Within Five Years - New Castle News
stories.Summary:
Everlaw, an AI litigation and investigations platform based in Oakland, California, released a survey on October 20, 2026, about how corporate legal departments use generative AI. The survey of 300 U.S. in-house legal professionals was conducted with Wakefield Research between June 26 and July 30, 2026. It found that 86 percent of in-house teams now use generative AI for legal work. According to the report, 54 percent of respondents whose departments use outside counsel say AI has already reduced the volume of work sent to law firms.

The survey reports that 81 percent of respondents expect outcome-based pricing to eclipse the billable hour within five years, including 47 percent who expect it within three years and 17 percent within 12 months. Among those who engage law firms, 62 percent expect clear disclosure of AI use, 61 percent expect measurable gains in efficiency or outcomes, and 60 percent expect lower fees or fewer billed hours when AI is used. Fifty-seven percent expect flat or fixed fees to be the most widely adopted alternative arrangement. The report also says 92 percent of respondents whose teams use generative AI report AI-related savings from outside counsel, with 13 percent describing the savings as significant and 56 percent as moderate.

Gloria Lee, Chief Legal Officer at Everlaw, said AI rebalances the relationship between in-house teams and their law firms. She said in-house teams can take control of certain types of work and act as strategic advisers on high-value challenges. Lee also said in-house teams have the motivation, which is cost savings, and the power, because they can already reduce their dependence on outside firms, to drive the shift to outcome-based billing. On risk, she said the erosion of legal skills is not something individuals can solve alone, and that law firms, clients, law schools and legal tech vendors all have a role in building training models.

The report also covers quality and risk. Seventy percent of those using or testing generative AI say it has improved accuracy and consistency in legal work. Respondents were more concerned about errors and misalignment, at 80 percent, and non-lawyers relying on generative AI for legal guidance, at 72 percent, than about other risks. One third have encountered AI-hallucinated evidence or case law in litigation, including 17 percent from opposing counsel and 12 percent from their own teams. Respondents still expect to pay law firms for judgment and expertise, with 56 percent saying clients should primarily pay outside counsel for business and commercial insight.

The NUS-ISS Annual Luncheon 2026 took place at Conrad Singapore Orchard on 19 October 2026, with the theme "IGNITE. INSPIRE. INNOVATE." Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi, Senior Parliamentary Secretary at the Ministry of Education and Ministry of National Development, was the Guest-of-Honour. The event brought together industry partners, alumni, learners and staff.

It also included the prize presentation for the NUS-ISS Show Me Your Agents Hackathon. The hackathon, powered by AWS and supported by the Singapore Business Federation, drew 440 participants across 114 teams. Ten finalist teams pitched at the Finale Demo Day on 10 October 2026, and Team Interns won the SME category while Questbond won the public category. Special awards sponsored by SBF went to Team MOSS, Team AI've Got This and Team Binary Beast.

NUS-ISS is also piloting the Active Learning for Problem Solving programme with SBF member companies, and its new part-time Master of Science in Enterprise Digital Technology Management will take its first intake in 2027. Mr Khoong Chan Meng, Chief Executive Officer of NUS-ISS, said the question for organisations is no longer whether to adopt AI but how to make it work for their people and business. He said organisations will need both technology capabilities and people capabilities to use AI meaningfully. He added that SMEs may face different challenges in making transformation happen.

He said the Hackathon and ALPS aim to give businesses practical chances to experiment, solve real problems and turn ideas into outcomes. The luncheon also highlighted industry partnerships, including NCS, whose employees have completed 1,706 Graduate Certificates since the partnership began in 2019, with 68 conferred a Master of Technology in 2026. ST Engineering has trained more than 800 employees since 2025 as it aims to grow its pool of AI engineers and developers from 2,000 to 5,000 over the next two years. NUS-ISS was established in 1981 and says close to 216,000 digital leaders and professionals from 8,854 corporate client organisations have benefited from its services.

stories.Headline: Assembly Committee Passes Chatbot User Protection Bill
stories.Summary:
The Assembly Public Safety and Preparedness Committee passed A-5607 on the morning of October 19, 2026, in Trenton. The bill tries to regulate chatbot providers against manipulative pattern matching behaviors. Assemblyman Joe Danielsen, a Democrat and the committee chair, said the bill takes all reasonable care to protect the chatbot user. Assemblyman Antwan McClellan, a Republican, opposed the bill.

The bill sets content and data privacy rules for chatbot providers. Providers could not process personal data beyond input data without a user's affirmative consent, could not sell a user's chat log, and could not keep a chat log longer than two years unless the law requires it. They would have to let users access and download their chat logs at any time, run a data security program, and assess the chatbot for risks of harm every month. A chatbot would count as a product under product liability law, and a provider that violates the bill would owe a civil penalty of $5,000 for each violation.

A harmed user could sue in Superior Court and win the greater of actual damages or $5,000 for each violation, plus reasonable attorney fees and court costs. Assemblyman Paul Kanitra, a Republican, compared supporters of the bill to cavemen trying to stomp out fire, and he eventually abstained. Assemblywoman Carol Murphy, a Democrat, said she had certain reservations but voted yes for now. Beverly Brown Ruggia of the Consumer Federation of America and NJ Citizen Action said all ages are impacted by manipulative chatbots.

She said chatbots are not people, straightforward rules can make them safer, and people cannot rely on promises by tech CEOs. The committee moved the bill while recognizing its limitations and the need for much deeper examination of the AI superhighway. Questions remained about how effective the bill would be, including a lack of clarity about its geographic scope. The articles do not say what happens next.
